newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Pennsylvania prison population on upward climb.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Pennsylvania prison population on upward climb.

text.p: The State Correctional Institution in Greene County, Pennsylvania, is so sparkling clean you can almost see your reflection in the coiled razor-sharp wire that surrounds the buildings.

The 1,650-bed facility, which employs 650 correctional professionals, is ringed by gleaming fences and equipped with ultra-sensitive metal detectors. Dedicated in 1993, it is already full and two new units with a combined capacity of about 500 are in the works.

SCI Greene is one product of a prison-building boom in Pennsylvania necessitated by a ballooning prison population. This is causing some state legislators who were fans of a "lock 'em up and throw away the key" anti-crime policy to crusade for alternative sentencing such as boot camps and rehabilitation programs.

"You can't build your way out of this problem," Stewart Greenleaf, a Republican state senator from Montgomery, said. Once a strident voice for mandatory sentencing, he is now a leading crusader for correctional reform.

Greenleaf said the state's correctional system is at 154 percent of capacity. He is pushing legislation calling for alternative punishment for nonviolent criminals and technical parole violators, expansion of existing "boot camp" programs, diversion of drug law violators into treatment centers rather than jail cells and privatization of prison management.

In 1980, Pennsylvania prisons housed some 8,000 inmates. The number currently hovers around 35,000 and a study by the state's Commission on Crime and Delinquency predicts it will swell to about 40,000 in less than ten years.
INCREASE IN PRISON POPULATION AMONG THE HIGHEST

Pennsylvania posted a 13.7 percent increase in its prison population from mid-1995 to mid-1996, according to the Bureau of Justice Statistics. Only five states had larger increases, Nebraska, Montana, North Carolina, Oregon and Wisconsin.
The estimated U.S. prison population in this period rose to 1,630,940 from 1,585,400.

The effect on Pennsylvania's budget has been a staggering increase in money for prisons. Gov. Tom Ridge's proposed fiscal 1997-98 budget includes $983 million for the Department of Corrections, more than 10 times the 1979-80 figure.

The budget includes millions of dollars for a new facility in Delaware County, conversion of a Somerset County hospital into a prison and construction of 11 new cell blocks at six existing institutions. Meanwhile, corrections employment has grown to 13,442, second only to the Department of Public Welfare among state agencies.

Some experts attribute the growing prison population to stepped-up drug enforcement that began in the mid-1980s. "(That) was a time when serious drug use was coming down," said Carnegie Mellon University criminology professor Alfred Blumstein. "But it was also a time of crack use and (law enforcement) was very aggressive at cracking down on that."
AVERAGE STAY IN PRISON IS UP

Every year, about 2,000 narcotics offenders are turned over to Pennsylvania prisons, about one-third of the system's annual freshmen class. Because of mandatory sentencing laws passed mostly in the 1980s, those offenders are doing more time, helping push the average length of stay in Pennsylvania prisons from 32 months in 1984 to 44 months in 1994.
Blumstein noted that offenders in incidents of domestic violence and related abuses also are ending up behind bars. "That was not a significant factor 25 years ago."

Also contributing to the behind-bars boom are lengthening sentences for murders and lower parole rates. Pennsylvania has not eliminated parole as other states have, but rates have dropped and parolees who violate the terms of their paroles -- often by failing a drug test -- are increasingly ending up back in prison rather than in rehabilitation programs.

Meanwhile, Greenleaf's proposals, contained in two bills, have been floating around the state legislature for more than a year, and Ridge has not stated a position on them. But Greenleaf has support from minority Democrats.

"We should return to allowing judges more discretion in sentencing," Democratic State Rep. William Robinson said. Saying the "lock 'em up" approach has been a failure, he supports boot camps, releasing some elderly prisoners and improving schools so fewer young people turn to crime.
"It's frightening to think that we're putting so much money in at the back end and so little on the front end," he said.
